title: Postgres Internals: How It Actually Works

blocks.title: The big picture
blocks.markdown:
Postgres looks like one program and behaves like a small operating system. A single **postmaster** process owns a shared memory segment; every client connection gets its own forked **backend** process; a handful of auxiliary processes handle durability and cleanup in the background.

Almost everything surprising about Postgres follows from one design decision: **it never modifies a row in place.** An UPDATE writes a new version of the row and marks the old one superseded. That single choice explains, in a chain:

- why readers never block writers and writers never block readers,
- why `UPDATE` can be slower than `INSERT`,
- why tables bloat and `VACUUM` has to exist,
- why a 32-bit transaction counter can threaten to shut your database down,
- why an index scan usually still has to touch the heap.

Underneath sits an equally simple durability rule — **write the log before the data** — from which checkpoints, crash recovery, point-in-time restore and streaming replication all fall out as the same mechanism wearing different hats.

This board works from the disk upward: the page, the tuple, visibility, the log, the cache, then the planner and executor that sit on top of all of it.

blocks.caption: Process-per-connection, not thread-per-connection. Backends are separate OS processes, so everything they share must live in one shared memory segment — and every access to it must be locked.

blocks.title: Process and memory architecture
blocks.tagline: A separate OS process per connection — which is why shared memory is the whole story.
blocks.markdown:
The **postmaster** starts first. It reads the configuration, allocates the shared memory segment, and forks the auxiliary processes. Then it mostly waits: for each new connection it forks a **backend** and hands the socket over.

That backend does *everything* for the session — reads the protocol stream, parses the SQL, plans it, executes it, manages the transaction, returns rows. There is no thread pool and no work-stealing scheduler. (Parallel query added worker processes for a single query, but the unit is still a process.)

### What this buys, and what it costs

A crashing backend can be reaped without taking down the server, and there is no shared heap to corrupt. The cost is that a connection is an OS process with its own page tables — which is precisely why a connection pooler stops being optional at a few hundred clients, and why `work_mem` is a **per-node, per-backend** budget rather than a global one. A query with four sorts, run by fifty backends, can allocate two hundred times `work_mem`.

### The shared parts

Because backends share no address space, everything collaborative lives in the shared memory segment: `shared_buffers`, the WAL buffers, the lock tables, the commit log. Nothing there is protected by language-level synchronization — it is guarded by **lightweight locks** taken by hand. That is why the lock manager is a first-class subsystem rather than an implementation detail.

The auxiliary processes are each doing one boring, essential job: the **background writer** trickles dirty buffers out so backends rarely have to write one themselves; the **checkpointer** does the heavy periodic flush; the **WAL writer** pushes the log out so commits find their work already done; the **autovacuum launcher** starts workers against tables that have accumulated enough dead rows.

blocks.title: The 8 KB page, and the indirection that matters
blocks.tagline: Every file is pages; every page is a tiny two-ended allocator.
blocks.markdown:
Heaps, indexes, the free space map and the visibility map are all the same shape on disk: a sequence of fixed-length pages, **8192 bytes** by default.

A page has four regions and grows from **both ends**:

| Region | Size | Grows |
|---|---|---|
| Page header | 24 bytes | fixed |
| Line pointer array | 4 bytes each | downward from the header |
| Free space | `pd_lower` → `pd_upper` | shrinks from both sides |
| Tuple data | variable | upward from the end |

Free space is not tracked in a structure — it is literally the gap between `pd_lower` and `pd_upper`.

### The load-bearing idea

A tuple's address, its **ctid**, is a `(block number, line pointer index)` pair — *not* a byte offset. Index entries store that pair. So the physical position of a tuple inside its page is free to change: Postgres can defragment a page, or point a line pointer at a different tuple, and every index still resolves correctly.

That one indirection pays for two major optimizations:

- **HOT updates** — if the new row version fits on the same page and no indexed column   changed, the old line pointer is turned into a redirect to the new tuple. **No index is   touched at all.** This is why `fillfactor` below 100 can dramatically cut index write   traffic on update-heavy tables: you are deliberately leaving room for the next version.
- **Page defragmentation** — VACUUM can compact live tuples toward the end of the page and   reclaim the holes without any index maintenance.

### Tuples and TOAST

Each tuple carries a header of 23 bytes (padded, so `t_hoff` is normally 24) holding `t_xmin`, `t_xmax`, `t_ctid` and the info-mask bits, followed by an optional null bitmap, then your data.

A tuple may not span pages. So when a row would exceed roughly 2 KB (a quarter page), **TOAST** takes over: oversized attributes are compressed, and if still too large, sliced into chunks in a side table, leaving an 18-byte pointer behind. This is invisible until it isn't — a `SELECT *` on a wide row silently reassembles those chunks, which is one of the more common sources of mysterious I/O.

blocks.title: MVCC: what a transaction is allowed to see
blocks.tagline: Two integers in every tuple header decide everything.
blocks.markdown:
Postgres keeps **multiple physical versions of the same logical row** and decides per transaction which one is real. The decision needs only two fields from the tuple header:

- **`t_xmin`** — the transaction that created this version
- **`t_xmax`** — the transaction that deleted or superseded it, `0` while live

### The snapshot

When a transaction needs a consistent view it takes a **snapshot**: the oldest still-running XID, the first not-yet-assigned XID, and the list of XIDs in flight right now. A version is visible when:

1. its `xmin` **committed**, and committed *before* the snapshot was taken, **and**
2. its `xmax` is zero, or aborted, or still in the snapshot's future.

Commit status is not in the tuple — it lives in the commit log (`pg_xact`). The first reader to check a tuple after commit caches the answer back into the tuple's info-mask **hint bits**, which is why the first `SELECT` after a big write can dirty pages and generate write I/O even though it changed nothing you asked about.

### UPDATE is DELETE + INSERT

There is no in-place update. The old version gets `xmax` set to the updating XID; a new version is inserted with `xmin` set to the same XID. Both sit on the page. Everything else follows:

- **Readers never block writers, writers never block readers.** They are looking at different   physical tuples, so no lock is needed between them.
- **Rollback is nearly free.** Aborting writes one byte in the commit log; the versions the   transaction created simply never become visible.
- **Dead versions pile up**, and something has to remove them. That is VACUUM.
- A dead version can only be removed once its `xmax` is older than the **oldest snapshot still   in use** in the entire cluster. One forgotten `BEGIN;` in a psql window pins that horizon   and stops cleanup on every table in the database. This is the single most common cause of   runaway bloat in production.

blocks.title: Watch MVCC decide — press Run
blocks.code:
"""The visibility rule that decides what every Postgres query can see."""

COMMITTED, ABORTED, RUNNING = "committed", "aborted", "running"

# The commit log (pg_xact / clog) — one status per transaction id.
clog = {100: COMMITTED, 101: COMMITTED, 102: RUNNING, 103: ABORTED}

class Snapshot:
    """What a transaction froze in time when it took its snapshot."""
    def __init__(self, xmin, xmax, in_progress):
        self.xmin = xmin                    # oldest still-running xid
        self.xmax = xmax                    # first xid not yet assigned
        self.in_progress = set(in_progress)

    def in_past(self, xid):
        """True if xid had already finished when the snapshot was taken."""
        if xid >= self.xmax:                # started after we did
            return False
        if xid in self.in_progress:         # running when we looked
            return False
        return True

def visible(tup, snap):
    xmin, xmax = tup["xmin"], tup["xmax"]
    # The version must have been created by a transaction that committed
    # in our past — otherwise it either never happened or is not ours to see.
    if clog.get(xmin) != COMMITTED or not snap.in_past(xmin):
        return False
    if xmax == 0:                           # never deleted: live
        return True
    # It was deleted — but only a delete that committed in our past hides it.
    if clog.get(xmax) != COMMITTED or not snap.in_past(xmax):
        return True
    return False

# One logical row, three physical versions — exactly what an UPDATE leaves behind.
heap = [
    {"label": "v1 'alice'   inserted by 100, superseded by 101", "xmin": 100, "xmax": 101},
    {"label": "v2 'ALICE'   inserted by 101, still live       ", "xmin": 101, "xmax": 0},
    {"label": "v3 'Alicia'  inserted by 102 (still running)   ", "xmin": 102, "xmax": 0},
    {"label": "v4 'oops'    inserted by 103 (rolled back)     ", "xmin": 103, "xmax": 0},
]

snap = Snapshot(xmin=102, xmax=104, in_progress=[102])
print(f"snapshot: xmin={snap.xmin} xmax={snap.xmax} in_progress={sorted(snap.in_progress)}\n")
for tup in heap:
    mark = "VISIBLE" if visible(tup, snap) else "  ---  "
    print(f"  [{mark}] {tup['label']}")

live = [t for t in heap if visible(t, snap)]
print(f"\n{len(heap)} versions on the page, {len(live)} visible -> SELECT returns "
      f"{len(live)} row. The other {len(heap) - len(live)} are VACUUM's problem.")
blocks.explanation: This is the actual rule, not an analogy: check `xmin` committed and in the past, then let `xmax` overrule it. Four physical versions of one logical row — the shape an UPDATE, a concurrent write and a rollback leave behind — and exactly one survives. Change the snapshot to `Snapshot(xmin=104, xmax=105, in_progress=[])` and run it again: transaction 102 has now committed in your past, and a different version wins.

blocks.title: The same thing, from psql
blocks.explanation: `pageinspect` is the honest way to check your mental model — it shows the raw line pointers and tuple headers of a page. The old version's `t_ctid` pointing at `(0,2)` is the update chain that lets a concurrent transaction follow a row forward.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram

  participant S as shared_buffers
  participant W as WAL buffer
  participant D as pg_wal on disk
  participant H as Heap on disk

  B->>D: COMMIT - fsync the WAL
  D-->>B: durable

blocks.caption: Commit is an fsync of the log, not of your table. The heap page may reach disk minutes later — or never, if the page is dirtied again first.

blocks.title: WAL: write the log before the data
blocks.tagline: One rule, from which durability, replication and PITR all follow.
blocks.markdown:
The **write-ahead rule**: a change must be described in the log, and that log flushed to durable storage, *before* the modified data page may be written.

So `COMMIT` means **the WAL record is on disk**. Your table's pages are still dirty in `shared_buffers`. This is why Postgres commits fast: it turns scattered random writes across many pages into one sequential append plus one `fsync`.

### LSNs

Every WAL record has a **log sequence number** — its byte offset in a conceptually infinite stream. Every page stores the LSN of the last record that modified it. Recovery compares the two: if a page's LSN is already at or beyond the record being replayed, that change is already there and gets skipped. That comparison is what makes replay **idempotent**, and therefore safe to crash in the middle of.

### Full page writes

The first time a page is modified after a checkpoint, its **entire 8 KB image** goes into the WAL, not just the delta.

The reason is torn pages. Your storage promises atomicity at its own sector size, not at 8 KB. Lose power mid-write and a page can land half old, half new — internally inconsistent in a way no delta record can repair, because a delta assumes a known starting state. A full image assumes nothing.

This is why WAL volume **spikes immediately after every checkpoint** and tapers off until the next one, and why checkpointing too often can cost more in write amplification than it saves in recovery time.

### The same log, three products

Crash recovery replays it locally. **PITR** archives it and replays to a chosen moment. **Streaming replication** ships it to another server that replays it continuously. A replica is not a special mode — it is a server permanently in recovery, reading someone else's log.

blocks.title: Checkpoints and crash recovery
blocks.tagline: A checkpoint is a promise about how far back recovery must read.
blocks.markdown:
A **checkpoint** flushes every dirty buffer to disk, then writes a checkpoint record containing the **redo point** — the LSN where recovery must begin. Everything before it is known durable.

### Recovery, in three steps

1. Read the control file, find the last checkpoint record, take its redo point.
2. Replay WAL forward from there. Each record either applies to its page or is skipped    because the page's LSN shows it already landed.
3. Restore any torn page from the full-page image the log is guaranteed to hold.

That is the whole algorithm. There is no undo pass — MVCC means an aborted transaction's rows simply never become visible, so there is nothing to roll back at recovery time.

### The tuning tension

`checkpoint_timeout` and `max_wal_size` decide how often checkpoints run, and the trade is direct:

- **Frequent checkpoints** — fast recovery, but more full page writes and repeated flushing of   the same hot pages.
- **Rare checkpoints** — less write amplification, but more WAL to replay after a crash, and a   larger burst of dirty pages when the checkpoint finally lands.

`checkpoint_completion_target` spreads the flushing across the interval rather than dumping it at the end, which is what keeps a checkpoint from showing up as a latency cliff. Watch `pg_stat_checkpointer`: checkpoints triggered by WAL volume rather than by time mean `max_wal_size` is too small for the workload.

blocks.title: VACUUM, freezing, and the wraparound clock
blocks.tagline: Cleanup is not housekeeping — it is a correctness requirement on a timer.
blocks.markdown:
VACUUM does three separate jobs, and it is worth keeping them apart:

1. **Reclaim dead tuples.** Plain VACUUM marks their space reusable *within the page*. It does    not return space to the operating system — only `VACUUM FULL` does, by rewriting the whole    table under an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock.
2. **Maintain the visibility map**, marking pages where every tuple is visible to everyone.    Index-only scans depend entirely on this.
3. **Freeze old rows** — and this one is not optional.

### Autovacuum's trigger

Roughly `50 + 0.2 × reltuples` changed rows. A 1,000-row table is vacuumed after ~250 changes; a 100-million-row table waits for **20 million**. The scale factor is why large tables are almost always under-vacuumed at default settings — lowering `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` for big tables is one of the highest-value knobs in Postgres.

### Wraparound

A transaction ID is **32 bits**. Postgres distinguishes past from future by *age*, comparing modulo 2³², so only about **2³¹ ≈ 2.1 billion** transactions of that space are usable at once. Let an unfrozen row get older than that and the arithmetic inverts: its `xmin` starts looking like it is in the *future*, and the row **disappears**.

Freezing is the defence. VACUUM stamps sufficiently old rows as unconditionally visible, retiring their XID from the comparison entirely. If freezing falls far enough behind, the server starts warning, then refuses to assign new XIDs at all — it stops accepting writes to protect your data from silently vanishing.

Monitor it with one query and never be surprised:

```sql
SELECT relname, age(relfrozenxid) AS xid_age
FROM   pg_class WHERE relkind = 'r'
ORDER  BY xid_age DESC LIMIT 10;
```

blocks.title: The wraparound clock is faster than it looks
blocks.caption: Arithmetic, not measurement: transaction rate × 86,400 × days. The flat line is the ~2.1 billion (2³¹) usable XID space. Where a workload line crosses it is when unfrozen rows would start reading as future rows — so freezing has to have finished before then.
blocks.markdown: A busy OLTP box at 3,000 transactions per second burns through the entire usable transaction ID space in **about eight days**. At 1,000/s it takes about 25. This is why autovacuum's freezing work is not something you can defer indefinitely on a large, hot table — and why `age(relfrozenxid)` belongs on your dashboard next to disk space.

blocks.title: Clock sweep: choosing a victim
blocks.caption: Not LRU — an approximation of it that needs no ordering and no list surgery on every access, which matters when dozens of processes touch the same array concurrently.

blocks.title: The buffer manager
blocks.tagline: A fixed array of 8 KB frames, an approximation of LRU, and one rule it can never break.
blocks.markdown:
`shared_buffers` is an array of page-sized frames plus, for each, a **`BufferDesc`** holding a reference count, a usage count and flags (dirty, valid, locked).

**Pinning.** `ReadBuffer()` increments the reference count, making the frame ineligible for eviction while someone is reading it; `ReleaseBuffer()` drops it. A pin is not a lock — two backends can pin the same buffer at once. Content locking is separate and finer-grained.

**Clock sweep.** Rather than maintaining true LRU order, a hand rotates over the array. At each frame: pinned → skip; usage count above zero → decrement and move on; zero → this is the victim. Frequently touched pages keep getting their count bumped back up on access, so they survive several revolutions. It is an approximation of LRU that costs one atomic decrement instead of moving a node in a shared list — which is the difference that matters when many processes hit the array concurrently.

**And the rule it cannot break:** if the victim is dirty, its WAL must be flushed before the page is written. Write-ahead logging is not just a commit-path concern — it constrains eviction too.

### Ring buffers

A sequential scan of a table larger than the cache would otherwise evict everything for pages it will never revisit. So large scans, `COPY`, and VACUUM use a small **ring** of frames (hundreds of kilobytes) and recycle it, leaving the rest of the cache alone. Your OLTP working set survives an analyst's full-table scan because of this, not by luck.

### Double caching

Postgres reads through the OS page cache and does not use direct I/O, so a hot page often exists **twice** in RAM. That is the reason for the folklore that `shared_buffers` should be around 25% of memory rather than most of it — you are deliberately leaving room for the kernel cache underneath. `pg_buffercache` will show you what is actually resident.

blocks.caption: Four stages. The planner is the only one that makes a judgement call — and it makes it from statistics, which is where plans go wrong.

blocks.title: Planner and executor
blocks.tagline: Cost-based search over plan shapes, then one uniform interface: give me the next tuple.
blocks.markdown:
### Planning

The planner builds **paths** — candidate ways to produce a result — and costs each one. For join ordering it does bottom-up dynamic programming: best path for each single relation, then each pair, and so on. That is exponential, so above **`geqo_threshold`** (default 12 `FROM` items) it hands over to **GEQO**, a genetic algorithm that samples the space instead of covering it. GEQO is not deterministic — the same query can get different plans on different runs, which is worth knowing before you spend an afternoon confused by it.

Costs are unitless, anchored to sequential I/O:

| Constant | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `seq_page_cost` | 1.0 | one page fetched sequentially |
| `random_page_cost` | 4.0 | one page fetched randomly |
| `cpu_tuple_cost` | 0.01 | processing one row |
| `cpu_index_tuple_cost` | 0.005 | processing one index entry |
| `cpu_operator_cost` | 0.0025 | one operator or function call |

That 4:1 random-to-sequential ratio was calibrated for spinning disks. On NVMe it is simply wrong, and leaving it there systematically biases the planner **away from index scans** — lowering `random_page_cost` to 1.1 is the single most common correct tuning change on modern storage.

### Why plans actually go wrong

Almost never the cost model. Almost always **cardinality estimation**. The planner estimates row counts from `pg_statistic` — histograms, most-common-value lists, and per-column distinct counts collected by `ANALYZE`. Critically, it assumes **columns are independent**. Given `WHERE city = 'Paris' AND country = 'France'` it multiplies two selectivities and predicts far fewer rows than exist, then picks a nested loop that is catastrophic at the real row count. `CREATE STATISTICS` exists precisely to teach it about correlated columns.

### Execution

The executor walks the plan as a tree of nodes in the **volcano / iterator** model: every node implements the same call — *give me the next tuple* — and pulls from its children. A sort node pulls everything before returning anything; a nested loop pulls one row from the outer side then rescans the inner. That single uniform interface is why arbitrarily complex plans compose from about forty node types, and why `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` can report `loops=N` on an inner node: you are seeing it restarted once per outer row.

blocks.title: Reading a plan like the planner wrote it
blocks.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS)
SELECT o.id, o.total
FROM   orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE  c.country = 'FR' AND o.created_at >= now() - interval '7 days';

-- Nested Loop  (cost=0.71..2140.55 rows=12 width=12)
--               (actual time=0.042..91.318 rows=48213 loops=1)
--   Buffers: shared hit=1428 read=38104
--   ->  Index Scan using customers_country_idx on customers c
--         (cost=0.29..18.4 rows=9 width=4) (actual rows=8422 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders o
--         (cost=0.42..235.6 rows=1 width=12) (actual rows=6 loops=8422)

-- Read it as three questions:
--   1. rows=12 estimated vs rows=48213 actual -> the estimate is off by 4000x.
--      Everything below is a consequence, not a separate problem.
--   2. loops=8422 -> the inner side was restarted 8422 times. A nested loop is
--      only correct when the outer side is tiny; the planner thought it was 9.
--   3. read=38104 -> pages that missed shared_buffers and went to the OS.

-- Why the estimate was wrong: country and customer activity are correlated,
-- and the planner assumes independence. Teach it otherwise:
CREATE STATISTICS orders_cust_stats (dependencies)
  ON customer_id, created_at FROM orders;
ANALYZE orders;
blocks.explanation: `BUFFERS` is the option most people never turn on and should always use — it separates "this plan is slow because it is doing too much work" from "this plan is slow because it is missing the cache." The habit worth building: compare `rows=` estimated against `rows=` actual **first**, before looking at timings. A plan is rarely bad; an estimate usually is.

blocks.title: Access methods, and what index-only really requires
blocks.tagline: Five index types, each answering a different shape of question.
blocks.markdown:
| Type | Answers | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **B-tree** | `=`, `<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`, prefix `LIKE`, and `ORDER BY` for free | the default; well-behaved |
| **Hash** | equality only | smaller than B-tree, but no ordering, no range |
| **GiST** | "contains / overlaps / is near" — geometry, ranges, k-NN | lossy: matches must be rechecked against the heap |
| **GIN** | membership inside a value — arrays, `JSONB`, full-text | large, slow to update, unbeatable for containment |
| **BRIN** | "which block ranges could hold this value" | tiny — kilobytes for a huge table — but only if physical order correlates |

BRIN is the one worth knowing about: on an append-only table of timestamped events, a BRIN index on the timestamp can be **thousands of times smaller** than the B-tree and nearly as effective, because rows arrive in roughly the order it summarizes. Shuffle that correlation and it degrades to useless.

### Index-only scans are not free

An index entry carries no visibility information — `xmin`/`xmax` live in the **heap** tuple. So even when an index contains every column a query needs, Postgres must normally visit the heap just to ask "is this row visible to me?"

The **visibility map** is the way out: one bit per heap page saying *every tuple on this page is visible to every transaction*. When the bit is set, the heap fetch is skipped. That bit is set by **VACUUM**.

Which produces a genuinely counter-intuitive result: **an index-only scan's performance depends on how recently you vacuumed.** A well-designed covering index on a table autovacuum has fallen behind on will still hit the heap for every row, and `EXPLAIN` will tell you so as `Heap Fetches: 48213`. If that number is large, the fix is vacuum, not the index.

blocks.title: Why a B-tree lookup costs the same at any scale
blocks.yLabel: index levels to reach a leaf
blocks.caption: Derived, not measured: ⌈log₍₂₀₀₎ N⌉, taking ~200 entries per 8 KB internal page for a typical integer key. The point is the shape — a thousandfold more rows costs one extra page read.
blocks.markdown: An 8 KB page holds on the order of 200 keys plus pointers, so each level multiplies the addressable rows by ~200. Going from ten thousand rows to ten *billion* — a factor of a million — costs **three extra page reads**, and the top levels are almost always cached. This is why "add an index" scales so well, and why the interesting cost of an index is never the lookup — it is the write amplification on every INSERT and non-HOT UPDATE.

blocks.title: Locking: three different mechanisms with confusingly similar names
blocks.markdown:
**Heavyweight locks** (the lock manager) guard tables and other objects. Eight modes, held to end of transaction, tracked in a shared hash table, and the only ones that participate in deadlock detection. `ALTER TABLE` taking `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` is why a schema migration can stall an entire application — and why it queues *behind* a long-running `SELECT` while everything else queues behind **it**.

**Lightweight locks (LWLocks)** guard shared-memory structures — buffer headers, WAL buffers, the commit log. Shared or exclusive, held for microseconds, and with **no deadlock detection**: safety comes from every code path taking them in the same fixed order. When you see `LWLock` in `pg_stat_activity.wait_event`, you are looking at internal contention, not application-level lock conflict.

**Row locks** live in the **tuple header itself**, not in a lock table. That is why Postgres can lock ten million rows without exhausting shared memory — a distinction from engines that escalate row locks to table locks under pressure. Four modes: `FOR KEY SHARE`, `FOR SHARE`, `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, `FOR UPDATE`.

**Deadlock detection is lazy.** No one is watching continuously. A transaction that has been waiting `deadlock_timeout` (1 second by default) wakes up and searches the wait-for graph for a cycle. So a deadlock always costs at least a second before anyone is aborted — and setting that timeout very low to "detect faster" instead burns CPU on graph searches during ordinary lock waits.

blocks.title: Reading the source, and where the truth actually lives
blocks.markdown:
Postgres is unusually approachable for a database engine, largely because the important directories carry `README` files that explain the design before you read a line of C.

- `src/backend/storage/buffer/README` — buffer manager, clock sweep, ring buffers
- `src/backend/storage/lmgr/README` — the lock manager and deadlock detection
- `src/backend/access/nbtree/README` — the B-tree implementation, including concurrency
- `src/backend/access/transam/README` — transactions, WAL, commit
- `src/backend/optimizer/README` — how paths are built and costed

Start with the README, then the header file, then the `.c`. The commit messages are also unusually good — `git log --follow` on a file you care about is a readable history of why the design is the way it is.

One habit that shortcuts a lot of guessing: **`pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type` and `wait_event` name the exact internal thing a backend is blocked on** — a specific LWLock, a buffer pin, an I/O. That column is the bridge from "the database is slow" to a named subsystem in the source tree.

blocks.caption: Eight subsystems. Every arrow you could draw between them ends up passing through either the page or the log.

entries.definition: Transaction ID. A 32-bit counter; only ~2³¹ of its space is usable at once, which is what makes freezing mandatory.
A tuple's physical address: (block number, line pointer index). Changes on every non-HOT update, which is why it is not a stable row identity.
Log sequence number — a byte position in the WAL stream. Stamped on every page, which is what makes replay idempotent.
A 4-byte slot in a page's array pointing at a tuple. The indirection that lets tuples move without touching indexes.
Heap-Only Tuple update: the new version fits on the same page and changed no indexed column, so no index is modified.
Cached commit status written back into a tuple's info-mask by the first reader after commit — why a pure SELECT can generate write I/O.
The oldest snapshot still in use across the cluster. VACUUM cannot remove anything newer, so one idle open transaction blocks all cleanup.
One bit per heap page: 'every tuple here is visible to everyone.' Set by VACUUM; index-only scans are impossible without it.
A per-relation fork tracking free space per page, so an INSERT can find a page with room without scanning.
The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique: compresses and slices values too large to fit a page into a side table.
An auxiliary file alongside a relation's main data file — the visibility map and free space map are forks.
The LSN recorded in a checkpoint where crash recovery must begin replaying.
The buffer eviction algorithm: a rotating hand decrements usage counts and takes the first unpinned buffer at zero.
Genetic Query Optimizer — the sampling join-order search used above geqo_threshold (12) FROM items. Non-deterministic.
The executor's design: every plan node exposes one operation, 'next tuple', and pulls from its children.
